findings.finding: 0% of trades were accepted even though the listener got it wrong; 7 of 44 words in use now started as a mistake (misheard, or coined for something else).
findings.evidence: Wrenford "kama" = wood: misheard: gama → kama (generation 14) · Wrenford "tate" = four: coined for "food" by Lark·16 (generation 16) · Oakhollow "kama" = wood: misheard: gama → kama (generation 14)

findings.q: Do the words used most change least?
findings.finding: Use vs. replacement rate across meanings: ρ = -0.65, p = 0.032, n = 12. Most used: two (8% replaced per generation), food (16% replaced per generation), tools (25% replaced per generation); least: four (48%), five (89%).
findings.evidence: Real languages show this (Pagel et al. 2007). n = meanings, so treat as suggestive.

findings.q: Do a few families take over, and does the language narrow with them?
findings.finding: By generation 23, every living agent descends from one founder. Families alive vs. distinct words per meaning across towns: ρ = 0.53, p = 0.005, n = 25.
findings.evidence: Children go to the best-placed parents, so lineages die out: a founder effect, as in population genetics. Caution: families and variety both fall over time, so the correlation may be the language converging, not the families narrowing it.
